Swarm Intelligence

Swarm Intelligence (SI) is the collective behavior of decentralized, self-organized systems, natural or artificial.
First introduced by G. Beni and J. Wang (1989), in the context of cellular robotic systems.
Swarm is a loosely structured collection of interacting agents, showing a collective behavior.
An agent is an autonomous entity which observes through sensors and acts upon an environment using actuators.
Example swarms are ant colonies, bee colonies, bird flocking, animal herding, crowd, etc.
Swarm Intelligence

SI systems consist typically of a population of simple agents interacting locally with one another and with their environment.
Agents (such as ants, birds, people) follow very simple rules, local, and to a certain degree random. Interactions between such agents lead to the emergence of intelligent global group behavior without centralized control indicating how individual agents should behave.
Advantages: scalable, flexible, robust, adaptable.
Some applications of swarm principles
Network routing, crowd simulation, distributed problem solving, forecasting, data mining, military/space, optimization, etc.
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)

Inspired by the flocking and schooling patterns of birds and fish (R. Eberhart and J. Kennedy,1995).

Bees Algorithm

Behavior of bees
Scout bees search randomly from one flower patch to another, looking for nectar/pollen.
The bees return to the hive, deposit nectar/pollen, and advertise the patch at the dance floor to perform a waggle dance, providing the following information:
Direction of flow patches (angle between the sun and the patch)
Distance from the hive (duration of the dance)
Quality rating (frequency of the dance)
Follower bees go after the dancer bee to the path to gather food efficiently. 
The same patch may be advertised in the waggle dance again by other bees, attracting more bees to the patches.
Ultimately a flower patch can be abandoned.
Bees algorithm emulates the behavior of real bees.
http://beesalgorithmsite.altervista.org/BeesAlgorithm.htm

A colony of honey bees can extend itself over long distances in multiple directions (e.g., 10km).

textBlocks: Ant Colony Optimization (ACO)

Ants are capable of finding the shortest path from the food source to their nest using a chemical substance called pheromone to guide their search.
An ant may start an random walk, looking for food, leaving pheromone to remember the trail.
A passing lost ant will follow a trail, depending on the quality of the pheromone laid on the ground as the ants move.
Random walk can be sometimes beneficial. 
Pheromone is evaporated. So the more ants follow a path the stronger the path becomes, attracting more ants.
ACO emulates the behaviour of real ants.

Pheromone trails: reconnect a broken line

This elementary behavior of real ants can be used to explain how they can find the shortest path that reconnects a broken line after the sudden appearance of an unexpected obstacle has interrupted the initial path.
Let us consider the following scenario:
Ants are moving on a straight line that connects a food source to their nest.

Those ants which are just in front of the obstacle cannot continue to follow the pheromone trail and therefore they have to choose between turning right or left. In this situation we can expect half the ants to choose to turn right and the other half to turn left.

Shortest path around an obstacle

Those ants which choose, by chance, the shorter
path around the obstacle will more rapidly reconstitute the interrupted pheromone trail compared to those which choose the longer path. Thus, the shorter path will receive a greater amount of pheromone per time unit and in turn a larger number of ants will choose the shorter path.
